documentNotes.title: INSTRUCTIONS
documentNotes.statement:
DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN

- Work Part A first. You have 90 minutes to complete all four problems.
- After you have completed Part A, you may take a break.
- Then work Part B. You have 90 minutes to complete both problems.
- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example,

  Doe, Jamie
  A1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. It may not be used in graphing mode. Calculators may not be shared. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas. You may use a ruler or straight edge.
- Questions with the same point value are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Good luck!

problems.title: A1
problems.statement: A satellite of mass $m$ is in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around a star of mass $M$.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the magnitude of the satellite’s momentum $p$? Express your answer in terms of given quantities and constants.
parts.statementAfter: In Parts b, c, and d you should express the impulse vector $\vec{I}$ in terms of the satellite’s original momentum vector $\vec{p}$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: We wish to give the satellite a single impulse of minimum possible magnitude, causing it to escape from the star. What impulse $\vec{I}_e$ is necessary?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: We wish to give the satellite a single impulse of minimum possible magnitude, causing it to crash into the star. What impulse $\vec{I}_{C0}$ is necessary if you neglect the radius of the star?

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Suppose that the star has a radius $R$. Now what impulse $\vec{I}_{CR}$ is necessary to crash the satellite into the star? Your answer should also involve the ratio $r/R$.

solution.statement:
a. Setting the mass times centripetal acceleration equal to the gravitational force
$$m\frac{v^2}{r} = G\frac{Mm}{r^2}.$$
Solving for speed
$$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}},$$
and multiplying by mass to get the momentum
$$p = mv = m\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$

b. To escape from the star the total energy must be at least zero. Writing the escape speed $v_e$,
$$\tfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - G\frac{Mm}{r} = 0.$$
Solving for $v_e$, and multiplying by mass to get the needed momentum,
$$p_e = mv_e = m\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}} = \sqrt{2}p.$$
This is greater than p above, so the impulse must be in the direction of $\vec{p}$.
$$\vec{I}_e = \vec{p}_e - \vec{p} = \left(\sqrt{2} - 1\right)\vec{p}$$

c. Since angular momentum $L = mvr$ must be conserved, the only way to crash into a star with $R = 0$ is with $L = 0$. The satellite’s momentum $mv_{C0}$ must be slowed to zero.
$$\vec{I}_{C0} = m\vec{v}_{C0} - \vec{p} = 0 - \vec{p} = -\vec{p}.$$

d. Letting $v_r$ be the new speed at orbital radius $r$ and $v_R$ be the speed at stellar radius $R$, angular momentum conservation yields
$$mv_r r = mv_R R.$$
Solving for $v_R$
$$v_R = v_r\frac{r}{R}. \qquad \mathrm{(A1\text{-}1)}$$
Mechanical energy is also conserved.
$$\tfrac{1}{2}mv_r^2 - G\frac{Mm}{r} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_R^2 - G\frac{Mm}{R}$$
Regrouping terms and canceling $m$,
$$G\frac{M}{R} - G\frac{M}{r} = \tfrac{1}{2}v_R^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}v_r^2.$$
Substituting (A1-1)
$$2GM\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{r}\right) = v_r^2\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2 - v_r^2$$
$$\frac{2GM}{rR}(r - R) = \frac{v_r^2}{R^2}\left(r^2 - R^2\right)$$
Multiplying by $R$ and dividing by $(r - R)$
$$\frac{2GM}{r} = \frac{v_r^2}{R}(r + R)$$
Solving for $v_r$ and multiplying by mass to get $p_r$,
$$p_r = mv_r = m\sqrt{\frac{2GMR}{r(r + R)}} = m\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}\sqrt{\frac{2}{1 + \frac{r}{R}}} = p\sqrt{\frac{2}{1 + \frac{r}{R}}}$$
This is less than the original orbital momentum. Finding the impulse,
$$\vec{I}_{CR} = \vec{p}_r - \vec{p} = \vec{p}\sqrt{\frac{2}{1 + r/R}} - \vec{p} = -\vec{p}\left(1 - \sqrt{\frac{2}{1 + r/R}}\right)$$

problems.title: A2
problems.statement: All of the numbered boxes represent resistors. Each one has resistance $R$.

figures.alt: Resistor network in the shape of a square standing on a corner with vertices A (left), B (top), C (right) and D (bottom). Resistors 1 (A–B), 3 (B–C), 6 (A–D) and 8 (D–C) form the sides; resistors 2 (B to centre), 7 (centre to D), 4 (A to centre) and 5 (centre to C) connect the vertices to the central node.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the equivalent resistance between points A and C?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the equivalent resistance between points A and B?

solution.statement:
a. By symmetry the current through resistor 1 and 3 is the same. No current branches off through resistor 2. Similarly no current flows through resistor 7. The circuit reduces to that shown to the right. Each branch has two resistors in series for a total series resistance of
$$R_t = 2R.$$
The three branches are in parallel, so the equivalent resistance is
$$\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{2R} + \frac{1}{2R} + \frac{1}{2R} = \frac{3}{2R}.$$
Therefore
$$R_{eq} = \frac{2}{3}R$$

b. By symmetry the current through resistor 2 and 4 is the same. The current through resistor 5 is the same as that through resistor 7. The circuit reduces to that shown below. The series combination 5 and 7 has resistance
$$R_{57} = 2R.$$
This combination is in parallel with 8.
$$\frac{1}{R_{857}} = \frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{2R} = \frac{3}{2R}.$$
This combination is in series with 3 and 6.
$$R_{368573} = R + R + \tfrac{2}{3}R = \tfrac{8}{3}R$$
This combination is in parallel with the two other branches.
$$\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{2R} + \frac{3}{8R} = \frac{15}{8R}$$
$$R_{eq} = \frac{8}{15}R$$

figures.alt: Reduced circuit for part a: between A and C three parallel branches, each of two resistors in series: 1 and 3, 4 and 5, 6 and 8.

Reduced circuit for part b between terminals B (top left) and A (bottom left): resistor 1 directly between B and A; the series pair 2 and 4 in parallel with it; resistor 3 along the top and resistor 6 along the bottom leading to the series pair 5 and 7 in parallel with resistor 8 on the right.

problems.title: A3
problems.statement: A conducting slab has infinite extent in the $x$ and $y$ directions and thickness $L$ in the $z$ direction as shown in Figure a above. The slab is centered at $z = 0$ and carries a uniform current density $\vec{J} = J\hat{i}$ where $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, and $\hat{k}$ are unit vectors in the $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure a
figures.alt: Cross-section of a shaded slab of thickness L (double arrow at left) extending indefinitely left and right (dashed edges); axes z up and y to the right from a point in the middle marked with a dot, labelled "x out of page".

figures.caption: Figure b
figures.alt: The same slab of thickness L with axes z and y and "x out of page"; above it a square loop of side a (both sides labelled a) carrying current I (arrow pointing down on its left), at a distance b above the top surface of the slab (double arrow b).

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ at all points.

answer.value: B = ½μ₀JL ĵ for z < −L/2; B = −μ₀Jz ĵ for −L/2 < z < L/2; B = −½μ₀JL ĵ for z > L/2

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: A square wire loop of side $a$ is placed a distance $b$ above the slab (as shown in Figure b above). The loop has unit normal vector $\hat{n} = \cos\theta\hat{i} + \sin\theta\hat{j}$ and applied current $I$. (Figure b depicts the special case $\theta = 0$.) What is the net force and the net torque on the loop as a function of $\theta$?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: The applied current $I$ is now removed from the loop described above and the current density in the slab $\vec{J} = J\hat{i}$ is reduced to zero over time $T$. The wire used to construct the loop has resistance per unit length $S$. How much charge flows through each cross section of the loop wire due to the reduction in current density?

solution.statement:
a. The slab has infinite extent in the $x$ and $y$ direction. Therefore the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ can depend at most on $z$. By the right hand rule and symmetry $\vec{B}$ is to the left for positive $z$ and to the right for negative $z$.
$$\vec{B} = -B(z)\hat{j} \qquad z > 0$$
$$\vec{B} = +B(z)\hat{j} \qquad z < 0$$
$\vec{B}$ can be found from Ampere’s law. To find $\vec{B}$ outside the slab, $z > L/2$, use the loop shown in Figure a. The loop segments parallel to the $z$ direction are perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ and will not contribute.
$$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_o I_{enc}$$
$$Bw + Bw = \mu_o(LwJ)$$
$$B = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o LJ \qquad \text{for } \lvert z\rvert > L/2.$$
To find $\vec{B}$ inside the slab, $z < L/2$, use the loop shown in Figure b. Once again, the loop segments parallel to the $z$ direction are perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ and will not contribute.
$$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_o I_{enc}$$
$$Bw + Bw = \mu_o(2zwJ)$$
$$B = \mu_o Jz \qquad \text{for } \lvert z\rvert < L/2.$$
Including the direction,
$$\vec{B} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o JL\hat{j} \qquad -L/2 > z,$$
$$\vec{B} = -\mu_o Jz\hat{j} \qquad +L/2 > z > -L/2,$$
$$\vec{B} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o JL\hat{j} \qquad z > L/2$$

b. In the region of the loop, $\vec{B}$ is uniform, $\vec{B} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o JL\hat{j}$. The force on the top segment is equal and opposite to the force on the bottom segment. The force on the left segment it equal and opposite to the force on the right segment. The net force on the loop is zero.
$$\vec{F}_{net} = 0.$$
The net torque is given by
$$\vec{\tau}_{net} = \vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}$$
where $\vec{\mu}$, the magnetic dipole moment is
$$\vec{\mu} = IA\hat{n} = Ia^2\left(\cos\theta\hat{i} + \sin\theta\hat{j}\right).$$
$$\vec{\tau}_{net} = Ia^2\left(\cos\theta\hat{i} + \sin\theta\hat{j}\right)\times\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o JL\hat{j}\right)$$
$$\vec{\tau}_{net} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o JLIa^2\left(\cos\theta\hat{i}\times\hat{j} + \sin\theta\hat{j}\times\hat{j}\right)$$
$$\vec{\tau}_{net} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o JLIa^2\cos\theta\hat{k}$$

c. $\vec{B}$ is uniform so the flux through the loop is
$$\Phi = \vec{B}\cdot A\hat{n} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o JL\hat{j}\cdot a^2\left(\cos\theta\hat{i} + \sin\theta\hat{j}\right)$$
$$\Phi = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o JLa^2\sin\theta$$
Using Faraday’s Law, the emf
$$\mathcal{E} = -\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_o La^2\sin\theta\frac{\Delta J}{\Delta t}.$$
The emf is also
$$\mathcal{E} = IR = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}R$$
where
$$R = (4a)S.$$
$$\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{2R}\mu_o La^2\sin\theta\frac{\Delta J}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{8aS}\mu_o La^2\sin\theta\frac{\Delta J}{\Delta t}.$$
Since $J$ has been reduced to zero over time $T$, the charge $Q$ flowing in time $T$ is
$$Q = \frac{\mu_o aLJ}{8S}\sin\theta$$

figures.caption: Figure a
figures.alt: Slab of thickness L with a rectangular Amperian loop of width w and height 2z straddling the whole slab; arrows along the top and bottom segments; field B arrow pointing left above the slab and right below it.

figures.caption: Figure b
figures.alt: Slab of thickness L with a rectangular Amperian loop of width w and height 2z lying inside the slab; field arrows B pointing left in the upper half and right in the lower half.

problems.title: A4
problems.statement:
An ideal gas has a heat capacity per unit mole at constant pressure of $C_\mathrm{P} = 41.9$ J/(mol·K) and a heat capacity per unit mole at constant volume of $C_\mathrm{V} = 33.5$ J/(mol·K). An 0.100-mole sample of this gas goes through the accompanying cycle. Process 1–>2 is isobaric (constant pressure), 2–>3 is adiabatic (no heat enters or leaves), and 3–>1 is isothermal (constant temperature).

| | |
|---|---|
| $T_1 = 300$ K | $T_2 = 400$ K |
| $V_1 = 0.0118\ \mathrm{m^3}$ | $V_2 = 0.0157\ \mathrm{m^3}$ |

figures.alt: P–V diagram (P vertical, V horizontal) of a cycle: horizontal isobar from point 1 to point 2 (arrow to the right), a steep adiabat from 2 down to point 3 (arrow downward), and an isotherm from 3 back up to 1 (arrow toward 1).

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the work done by the gas during each process ($W_{1\text{–>}2}$, $W_{2\text{–>}3}$, and $W_{3\text{–>}1}$).

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the efficiency of this cycle?

solution.statement:
a. Process $1\to 2$ takes place at constant pressure. The work done is
$$W_{1\to 2} = p\Delta V.$$
For a constant pressure process, the ideal gas law yields $p\Delta V = nR\Delta T$
and
$$W_{1\to 2} = nR\Delta T = (0.10\ \mathrm{mol})(8.31\ \mathrm{J/mol\cdot K})(400\ \mathrm{K} - 300\ \mathrm{K}) = +83.1\ \mathrm{J}.$$

Process $2\to 3$ is adiabatic, $Q = 0$. Combining this with the first law of thermodynamics,
$$Q = W + \Delta U.$$
The work done is the negative of the change in internal energy.
$$W_{2\to 3} = -\Delta U = -nC_V\Delta T = -nC_V\left(T_3 - T_2\right).$$
Since process $3\to 1$ is isothermal, $T_3 = T_1 = 300\ \mathrm{K}$.
And
$$W_{2\to 3} = -(0.10\ \mathrm{mol})(33.5\ \mathrm{J/mol\cdot K})(300\ \mathrm{K} - 400\ \mathrm{K}) = +335\ \mathrm{J}.$$

For the isothermal process $3\to 1$, the work done is
$$W_{3\to 1} = nRT\ln\left(\frac{V_1}{V_3}\right).$$
Since $2\to 3$ is adiabatic,
$$p_2V_2^{\gamma} = p_3V_3^{\gamma}$$
with $\gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} = \frac{41.9}{33.5} = \frac{5}{4}$. Combining this with the ideal gas law $pV = nRT$,
$$nRT_2V_2^{\gamma-1} = nRT_3V_3^{\gamma-1}.$$
Solving for $V_3$,
$$V_3^{\gamma-1} = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_3}\right)V_2^{\gamma-1}$$
$$V_3 = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_3}\right)^{1/(\gamma-1)}V_2 = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_3}\right)^4V_2 = \left(\frac{400}{300}\right)^4\left(0.0157\ \mathrm{m^3}\right) = 0.0496\ \mathrm{m^3}$$
Finally,
$$W_{3\to 1} = (0.10\ \mathrm{mol})(8.31\ \mathrm{J/mol\cdot K})(300\ \mathrm{K})\ln\left(\frac{0.0118}{0.0496}\right) = -358\ \mathrm{J}.$$

b. The efficiency is the total work done divided by the heat input. Heat is input during process $1\to 2$ and leaves during $3\to 1$.
$$Q_{in} = Q_{1\to 2} = nC_p\Delta T = (0.10\ \mathrm{mol})(41.9\ \mathrm{J/mol\cdot K})(100\ \mathrm{K}) = +419\ \mathrm{J}$$
$$W_{net} = W_{1\to 2} + W_{2\to 3} + W_{3\to 1} = +83\ \mathrm{J} + 335\ \mathrm{J} - 358\ \mathrm{J} = 60\ \mathrm{J}$$
$$e = \frac{60}{419} = 0.14$$

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: In classical mechanics, the kinetic energy $K$, momentum $p$, and mass $m$ of a particle are related by $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$. Derive the relationship between the total energy $E$, momentum $p$, and mass $m$ of a particle in special relativity?
parts.statementAfter:
Hint: Express $E^2$ in terms of $p^2$. In addition to $m$, the expression may also include $c$. Relativistic expressions for the total energy $E$ and momentum $p$ of a particle of mass $m$ moving at speed $v$ are
$$E = \frac{mc^2}{\sqrt{1 - (v/c)^2}} \qquad\qquad p = \frac{mv}{\sqrt{1 - (v/c)^2}}$$

Particle A (mass $1000\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$) is at rest at the center of a spherical gamma detector, which completely surrounds it except for a small hole. We accelerate particle B (mass $500\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$) to a total energy of $700\ \mathrm{MeV}$, sending it through the hole towards particle A. When the particles collide, a single, excited particle of unknown mass, C\*, is produced. C\* quickly decays to its unexcited state, C (mass $1300\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$), emitting a single gamma ray.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find the mass of C\*.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: If the gamma is emitted directly away from the hole, what energy does the detector record?

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: The experiment is repeated, and the detector records an energy of $300\ \mathrm{MeV}$. At what angles did particle C and the gamma emerge? Assume that C\* decays at the center of the detector. Let an angle of 0 be directly away from the hole, and an angle of $\pi$ be directly towards the hole.

answer.value: gamma at 1.365 rad and C at 0.601 rad from the axis, on opposite sides of the axis

solution.statement:
a. Squaring the relativistic expressions for $E$ and $p$,
$$E^2 = \frac{m^2c^4}{1 - (v/c)^2} \qquad\qquad p^2 = \frac{m^2v^2}{1 - (v/c)^2}.$$
Multiplying the $p^2$ equation by $c^2$ and subtracting from $E^2$
$$E^2 - c^2p^2 = \frac{m^2c^4}{1 - (v/c)^2} - \frac{m^2v^2c^2}{1 - (v/c)^2} = \frac{m^2c^4\left(1 - (v/c)^2\right)}{1 - (v/c)^2} = m^2c^4$$
$$E^2 = (cp)^2 + \left(mc^2\right)^2$$

b. Since A is at rest, $E_A = m_Ac^2 = 1000\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $p_A = 0$;
and
$$cp_B = \sqrt{E_B^2 - m_B^2c^4} = \sqrt{(700\ \mathrm{MeV})^2 - (500\ \mathrm{MeV})^2} = 490\ \mathrm{MeV}.$$
By conservation of energy and momentum,
$$E_{C*} = E_A + E_B = 1000\ \mathrm{MeV} + 700\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1700\ \mathrm{MeV}$$
$$cp_{C*} = cp_A + cp_B = 0 + 490\ \mathrm{MeV} = 490\ \mathrm{MeV}$$
Thus
$$m_{C*}c^2 = \sqrt{E_{C*}^2 - (cp_{C*})^2} = \sqrt{(1700\ \mathrm{MeV})^2 - (490\ \mathrm{MeV})^2} = 1628\ \mathrm{MeV}.$$

c. Again, using conservation of energy and momentum,
$$E_C + E_\gamma = E_{C*}$$
$$cp_C + cp_\gamma = cp_{C*}$$
Since the gamma is massless, $E_\gamma^2 = (cp_\gamma)^2$. It is emitted along the direction of travel of C\*, so we select the positive root, $cp_\gamma = E_\gamma$. Thus, rearranging,
$$E_C = E_{C*} - E_\gamma$$
$$cp_C = cp_{C*} - E_\gamma$$
We need a fourth relationship,
$$E_C^2 - (cp_C)^2 = \left(m_Cc^2\right)^2.$$
$$\left(E_{C*} - E_\gamma\right)^2 - \left(cp_{C*} - E_\gamma\right)^2 = \left(m_Cc^2\right)^2$$
$$E_{C*}^2 - 2E_{C*}E_\gamma + E_\gamma^2 - (cp_{C*})^2 + 2cp_{C*}E_\gamma - E_\gamma^2 = \left(m_Cc^2\right)^2$$
$$E_{C*}^2 - (cp_{C*})^2 + 2cp_{C*}E_\gamma - 2E_{C*}E_\gamma = \left(m_Cc^2\right)^2$$
Since
$$E_{C*}^2 - (cp_{C*})^2 = \left(m_{C*}c^2\right)^2,$$
the prior equation becomes,
$$\left(m_{C*}c^2\right)^2 - 2E_\gamma\left(E_{C*} - cp_{C*}\right) = \left(m_Cc^2\right)^2$$
$$E_\gamma = \frac{\left(m_{C*}c^2\right)^2 - \left(m_Cc^2\right)^2}{2\left(E_{C*} - cp_{C*}\right)} = \frac{(1628\ \mathrm{MeV})^2 - (1300\ \mathrm{MeV})^2}{2(1700\ \mathrm{MeV} - 490\ \mathrm{MeV})} = 397\ \mathrm{MeV}$$

d. Let the gamma be emitted at an angle $\theta_\gamma$ to the axis, and C at an angle $\theta_C$. We measure the two angles on opposite sides of the axis so that both are in the interval $[0, \pi]$.
From conservation of energy,
$$E_C = E_{C*} - E_\gamma = 1700\ \mathrm{MeV} - 300\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1400\ \mathrm{MeV};$$
thus
$$cp_C = \sqrt{E_C^2 - \left(m_Cc^2\right)^2} = \sqrt{(1400\ \mathrm{MeV})^2 - (1300\ \mathrm{MeV})^2} = 520\ \mathrm{MeV}$$
And again,
$$cp_\gamma = E_\gamma = 300\ \mathrm{MeV}.$$
Then from conservation of momentum,
$$p_\gamma\sin\theta_\gamma - p_C\sin\theta_C = 0$$
$$p_\gamma\cos\theta_\gamma + p_C\cos\theta_C = p_{C*}$$
Rearranging,
$$\left(p_C\sin\theta_C\right)^2 + \left(p_C\cos\theta_C\right)^2 = \left(p_\gamma\sin\theta_\gamma\right)^2 + \left(p_{C*} - p_\gamma\cos\theta_\gamma\right)^2$$
$$p_C^2 = p_{C*}^2 + p_\gamma^2 - 2p_{C*}p_\gamma\cos\theta_\gamma$$
$$\cos\theta_\gamma = \frac{p_{C*}^2 + p_\gamma^2 - p_C^2}{2p_{C*}p_\gamma} = \frac{(490\ \mathrm{MeV/c})^2 + (300\ \mathrm{MeV/c})^2 - (520\ \mathrm{MeV/c})^2}{2(490\ \mathrm{MeV/c})(300\ \mathrm{MeV/c})} = 0.204$$
$$\theta_\gamma = \cos^{-1}0.204 = 1.365\ \mathrm{rad}.$$
Then,
$$\sin\theta_C = \frac{p_\gamma}{p_C}\sin\theta_\gamma = \frac{300\ \mathrm{MeV/c}}{520\ \mathrm{MeV/c}}\sin 1.365 = 0.565$$
Thus,
$$\theta_C = 0.601\ \mathrm{rad}.$$

problems.title: B2
problems.statement: A spherical container of radius $R$ is filled with a light, incompressible fluid carrying uniform charge density $\rho$. Let a point inside the container be described by $\vec{r} = r\hat{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ where the origin is at the center of the container and $\hat{r}$, $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, and $\hat{k}$ are unit vectors in the radial, $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions, respectively.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the electrostatic field inside the container.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: A small amount of fluid is replaced with a small, uncharged ball with mass density $\delta$ which is much, much greater than the fluid density. There is no gravitational field present. Ignore energy loss due to drag, and ignore any magnetic fields created by the moving fluid. Suppose that at time $t = 0$ the ball is released from rest at $\vec{r}_0 = x_0\hat{i}$, $x_0 < R$. What is $\vec{r}(t)$?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Repeat Part b, if there is a uniform gravitational field $\vec{g} = g\hat{i}$. Assume that $g$ is small enough so that the ball does not hit the wall of the container.
parts.statementAfter: d. The external gravitational field is removed, and the ball is again placed at $\vec{r}_0 = x_0\hat{i}$. Now, however, we start the ball with some nonzero velocity $\vec{v}_0 = v_0\hat{j}$.

parts.label: d. i.
parts.statement: What is the ball’s trajectory (before it hits the wall, if it does)? That is, what is the time-independent relationship between the ball’s $x$ and $y$ coordinates? Give the name of this trajectory, e.g. straight line, parabola, spiral…

parts.label: d. ii.
parts.statement: Is it possible for the ball to avoid the wall of the container? If so, what condition(s), if any, are required of $x_0$ and $v_0$?

answer.value: Yes, as long as v0 < ωR (x0 < R is given).

parts.label: d. iii.
parts.statement: If you answered “yes”, is the ball’s orbit periodic when it avoids the wall, and if so, what is the period? If you answered “no”, what is the maximum time that can elapse before it hits the wall?

solution.statement:
a. The field is spherically symmetric and radially oriented. Applying Gauss’s Law to a sphere of radius $r$,
$$\oint \vec{\mathrm{E}}\cdot d\vec{\mathrm{S}} = \frac{q_{encl}}{\varepsilon_0}$$
$$4\pi r^2E(r) = \frac{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\rho}{\varepsilon_0}$$
Therefore
$$\vec{E}(r) = \frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\vec{r}$$

b. Consider the small amount of fluid before it is replaced by the ball. It is in equilibrium. The electrostatic force $\vec{F}_E$ on the small amount of fluid due to the field is balanced by a force exerted by the rest of the fluid which we shall call an electrostatic buoyant force $\vec{F}_B$.
$$\vec{F}_B + \vec{F}_E = 0$$
$$\vec{F}_B = -\vec{F}_E = -q\vec{E} = -(\rho V)\left(\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\vec{r}\right) = -\frac{\rho^2V}{3\varepsilon_0}\vec{r}$$
where $V$ is the volume. When the fluid is replaced by the ball, there is no longer an electrostatic force on it and the buoyant force $\vec{F}_B$ is unbalanced and the net force acting on the ball. Using Newton’s second law with $m = \delta V$,
$$\delta V\vec{a} = -\frac{\rho^2V}{3\varepsilon_0}\vec{r}$$
$$\vec{a} = -\frac{\rho^2}{3\varepsilon_0\delta}\vec{r}. \qquad \mathrm{(B2\text{-}1)}$$
The motion is simple harmonic motion. Examining the initial conditions, the motion is one-dimensional in the $x$ direction. $\vec{r}(t) = x(t)\hat{i}$.
$$a_x = -\left(\frac{\rho^2}{3\varepsilon_0\delta}\right)x.$$
$$x(t) = x_0\cos\omega t \qquad \text{where} \qquad \omega = \frac{\rho}{\sqrt{3\varepsilon_0\delta}}.$$
and
$$\vec{r}(t) = x_0\hat{i}\cos\omega t,$$

c. Now the net force is
$$\vec{F} = -\frac{\rho^2}{3\varepsilon_0}V\vec{r} + mg\hat{i}$$
Since the ball is once again released from rest at $\vec{r}_0 = x_0\hat{i}$, the motion is once again one-dimensional in the $x$ direction. $\vec{r}(t) = x(t)\hat{i}$ and
$$ma_x = -\frac{\rho^2}{3\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{m}{\delta}\right)x + mg = -m\omega^2\left(x - \frac{g}{\omega^2}\right)$$
Letting $x' = x - \frac{g}{\omega^2}$, and noting that $a_{x'} = a_x$,
$$a_{x'} = -m\omega^2x'$$
i.e., $x'$ undergoes simple harmonic motion with the same frequency. Again, examining the initial conditions, we must have
$$x'(t) = x'(0)\cos\omega t = \left(x_0 - \frac{g}{\omega^2}\right)\cos\omega t$$
i.e.
$$x(t) = \left(x_0 - \frac{g}{\omega^2}\right)\cos\omega t + \frac{g}{\omega^2}$$
$$\vec{r}(t) = \left[\left(x_0 - \frac{g}{\omega^2}\right)\cos\omega t + \frac{g}{\omega^2}\right]\hat{i}$$

d. (i) Returning to equation (B2-1)
$$\vec{a} = -\frac{\rho^2}{3\varepsilon_0\delta}\vec{r} = -\omega^2\vec{r} \qquad \text{where} \quad \omega = \frac{\rho}{\sqrt{3\varepsilon_0\delta}}$$
Writing
$$\vec{r}(t) = x(t)\hat{i} + y(t)\hat{j} + z(t)\hat{k}$$
yields a separate simple harmonic motion equation for each component
$$a_x = -\omega^2x \qquad a_y = -\omega^2y \qquad a_z = -\omega^2z$$
The direction of the ball’s initial displacement is $\vec{r}_0 = x_0\hat{i}$, and the direction of its initial velocity is $\vec{v}_0 = v_0\hat{j}$. Examining these initial conditions, we must have
$$x(t) = x_0\cos\omega t \qquad y(t) = \frac{v_0}{\omega}\sin\omega t \qquad z(t) = 0.$$
Eliminating $t$, we have
$$\frac{x(t)^2}{x_0^2} + \frac{\omega^2y(t)^2}{v_0^2} = \cos^2\omega t + \sin^2\omega t = 1.$$
Therefore the path is an **ellipse**.

(ii) The maximum radius reached by the ball is the semimajor axis of the ellipse, which is the greater of $x_0$ and $\frac{v_0}{\omega}$. Since we know that $x_0 < R$, we only need $\frac{v_0}{\omega} < R$ for the ball to avoid the wall; that is, the ball **can** avoid the wall so long as $v_0 < \omega R$.

(iii) Since $x$, $y$, and $z$ all oscillate at the same frequency, the orbit must be **periodic** with that frequency, i.e. with period $\frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\frac{\sqrt{3\varepsilon_0\delta}}{\rho}$.
